overview: Alexander ruled Macedonia from 336 to 323 BCE and conquered an empire reaching from the eastern Mediterranean through Egypt and Iran to the Indus region. The imported map’s single outline runs from 323 to 300 BCE, beginning in Alexander’s death year. It sketches the conquests, not a united empire he continued to rule.

periods.title: Macedonian kingship
periods.summary: Alexander secured his inherited position before invading Asia.

items.text: Alexander crossed into Asia in 334 BCE. Victories over Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela opened the way to Babylon, Susa and the Persian royal heartland. Existing provincial structures often remained useful to the new ruler. Even so, a conquered region’s colour on a map can conceal places where resistance continued or effective royal control was limited.

Conquest also destroyed lives and places. Tyre resisted a prolonged siege and was devastated; Alexander’s forces later reached Persepolis, where the royal buildings burned in 330 BCE. These losses belong beside the stories of victories and cultural exchange. The empire’s growth was not experienced as a triumph by everyone within it.

A letter to Chios from 332 BCE ordered the return of exiles and the restoration of democracy. It also required the island to supply twenty warships with crews at its own expense and support a royal garrison until reconciliation. Local self-government therefore came with substantial military obligations and royal supervision.

At Tegea, regulations connected with Alexander’s recall of exiles in 324 BCE tried to settle a very practical problem: who owned a returning family’s home? The text discusses inherited property, women’s claims and gardens beside houses. It also sets deadlines for lawsuits. Coming home after political exile could mean complicated negotiations with the people already living there.

A contemporary inscription records Cyrene supplying grain during a shortage in Greece, around 330 to 326 BCE. Recipients included Athens and many other cities, as well as Alexander’s mother Olympias and his sister Cleopatra. This is evidence of food distribution and the royal women’s connections; it does not mean those enormous deliveries were simply their personal dinner supplies.

A supplies account from Bactria survives on leather nearly half a metre wide. It begins in June 324 BCE and continues for three months, dating its entries by Alexander’s reign while using Aramaic. The lower part is badly damaged, but the object still shows scribes doing the everyday work of recording supplies after conquest changed the name of the ruler.

At Susa in 324 BCE, Alexander arranged marriages linking Macedonian officers with Iranian noble families. Arrian describes bridegrooms seated for a banquet, brides being brought in, and the king providing dowries. Family relationships were being used to build political alliances. This is a later historian’s account of a royal event, rather than a description of everybody’s wedding.

Arrian also says Alexander offered to pay his soldiers’ debts. Some men were suspicious: writing down what they owed might reveal that they had overspent their pay. The king then allowed creditors to receive payment without the soldiers having to register their names. Even in a conquering army, money worries could follow people from one camp to the next.

Before he became king, Alexander studied with Aristotle at Mieza alongside other aristocratic youngsters. Archaeologists have uncovered a large gymnasium there with a courtyard, colonnades and rooms interpreted as dining halls. Its identification as the school is a modern scholarly proposal; the nearby caves once widely presented as Aristotle’s classroom are no longer the only candidate.

Plutarch says Alexander loved reading, requested books when they were hard to obtain on campaign, and kept a copy of the Iliad near his pillow. He also credits Alexander with an interest in medicine and advising sick friends about treatment. These are accounts written centuries afterward, useful for understanding his remembered interests without treating every anecdote as a contemporary medical record.

A silver tetradrachm in the British Museum, dated to Alexander’s reign, weighs 17.21 grams. One side shows Herakles; the other has Zeus seated with an eagle and sceptre. These were images of gods and heroes that users could recognize on a small object. The catalogue leaves this particular coin’s mint uncertain, so its precise place of manufacture should remain open.

Babylonian scholars kept watching the sky and recording earthly matters during Alexander’s rule. A diary for his final month includes commodity prices as well as planetary observations; missing pieces interrupt the entries. It puts the king’s death beside the work of measuring, observing and keeping accounts. A surviving related fragment in the British Museum is only six centimetres high.

An inscription from Athena’s temple at Priene reads “ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ ΑΛΕΞΑΝΔΡΟΣ ΑΝΕΘΗΚΕ ΤΟΝ ΝΑΟΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΗΙ ΠΟΛΙΑΔΙ”: “King Alexander dedicated the temple to Athena Polias.” The Greek comes from a surviving stone dedication of his reign. Spaces have been added to the capital-letter transcription for reading. The short message connects the king with a city’s goddess without proving that he personally designed or built the whole temple.

ending.text: Alexander died in Babylon in June 323 BCE. His death began a struggle over the kingship and territories, rather than an orderly handover to three ready-made countries. Over the following decades, successor dynasties established kingdoms including the Ptolemies, Seleucids and Antigonids. Communities, trade and scholarship continued through these political upheavals; the later Hellenistic world grew from both older regional traditions and the connections intensified by conquest.
